title: Lung adenocarcinomas with mucinous histology: clinical, genomic, and immune microenvironment characterization and outcomes to immunotherapy-based treatments and KRASG12C inhibitors
author: A Di Federico; L Hong; A Elkrief; R Thummalapalli; A J Cooper; B Ricciuti; S Digumarthy; J V Alessi; P Gogia; F Pecci; M Makarem; M M Gandhi; E Garbo; A Saini; A De Giglio; V Favorito; S Scalera; L Cipriani; D Marinelli; D Haradon; T Nguyen; J Haradon; E Voligny; V Vaz; F Gelsomino; F Sperandi; B Melotti; M Ladanyi; J Zhang; D L Gibbons; J V Heymach; M Nishino; J Lindsay; S J Rodig; K Pfaff; L M Sholl; X Wang; B E Johnson; P A Jänne; N Rekhtman; M Maugeri-Saccà; R S Heist; A Ardizzoni; M M Awad; K C Arbour; A J Schoenfeld; N I Vokes; J Luo
text:
Abstract
Background
Approximately 10% of lung adenocarcinomas (LUAD) have mucinous histology (LUADMuc), which is associated to a light/absent smoking history and a high prevalence of KRAS mutations. We sought to characterize LUADMuc by comparing it to LUAD without mucinous histology (LUADnon-muc) and determine the relative benefit of current treatments.
Patients and Methods
Patients with LUAD from five institutions and TCGA PanCancer Atlas classified as LUADMuc or LUADnon-muc were included. Clinicopathologic, genomic, immunophenotypic, transcriptional features, and treatment outcomes were compared between LUADMuc and LUADnon-muc.
Results
Of 4,082 patients with LUAD, 9.9% had LUADMuc. Compared to LUADnon-muc, patients with LUADMuc had a lighter smoking history (median: 15 vs 20 pack-years, P=0.008), lower PD-L1 TPS (median: 0% vs 5%, P<0.0001), and lower tumor mutation burden (median: 6.8 vs 8.5 mutations/megabase, P<0.0001). Mutations in KRAS, NKX2–1 (TTF-1), STK11, SMARCA4, GNAS, and ALK rearrangements were enriched in LUADMuc, while TP53, EGFR, BRAF, and MET mutations were enriched in LUADnon-muc. At stage IV diagnosis, LUADMuc was more likely to have contralateral lung metastasis (55.2% vs 36.9%, P<0.0001) and less likely to have brain metastases (23.3% vs 41.9%, P<0.0001). Compared to LUADnon-muc, LUADMuc cases showed lower intratumor CD8+, PD-1+, CD8+PD-1+, and FOXP3+ cells. Among metastatic cases receiving ICIs, compared to LUADnon-muc (N=1,511), LUADMuc (N=112) had lower objective response rate (ORR, 8.4% vs 25.9%, P<0.0001), and shorter median progression-free survival (mPFS, 2.6 vs 3.9 months, P<0.0001) and overall survival (mOS, 9.9 vs 17.2 months, P<0.0001). Similarly, patients with LUADMuc had worse outcomes to chemo-immunotherapy. LUADMuc (N=18) and LUADnon-muc (N=150) had similar ORR (16.7% vs 34.9%, P=0.12) and mPFS (4.6 vs 5.6 months, P=0.17) to treatment with KRASG12C inhibitors, but LUADMuc had shorter mOS (6.8 vs 10.8 months, P=0.018).
Conclusion
LUADMuc represents a distinct LUAD subpopulation with unique clinicopathologic, genomic, immunophenotypic, and transcriptional features, achieving worse outcomes to standard immunotherapy-based treatments.
Keywords: Non-small cell lung cancer, mucinous lung adenocarcinoma, histology, immunotherapy, KRAS inhibitors, genomics
Introduction
Among lung adenocarcinomas (LUAD), 3–10% of cases have a mucinous component (LUADMuc). LUADMuc is a World Health Organization (WHO)-recognized subtype of LUAD that is defined by goblet or columnar cells and abundant intracellular and extracellular mucin.4–8 Thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1) protein staining, which is typically positive in LUAD by immunohistochemistry (IHC), is frequently faint or negative in LUADMuc.9 Compared to patients with LUAD lacking a mucinous component (LUADnon-muc), patients with LUADMuc more frequently have a never smoking history. Patients with early-stage LUADMuc have a tendency to recur with intrapulmonary metastasis rather than distant metastasis.9,10 In addition, multiple clonally related spatially separate lung lesions involving one or both lungs are a common radiologic finding in LUADMuc cases.11 LUADMuc more frequently harbor KRAS driver mutations, which is generally associated with a more aggressive form of NSCLC, and driver NRG1 fusions.7,12,13 The efficacy of current standard therapies in patients with advanced LUADMuc remains to be elucidated.
Additionally, the emergence of new non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) targeted therapies (e.g. U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval of KRASG12C inhibitors in 2021) has increased the use of pathology and genomics biomarkers to predict immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) benefit (e.g. PD-L1 tumor proportion score [TPS] as a continuous biomarker). Further research is needed to define response to treatment in NSCLC subsets.1–3
We hypothesized that LUADMuc has distinctive clinical, pathologic, biologic, and genomic features with different sensitivity to existing treatments within LUAD. We sought to test this by comparing LUADMuc and LUADnon-muc in several patient cohorts from multiple institutions. In addition, the outcomes to therapies currently used for patients with advanced NSCLC, including ICI with or without chemotherapy and KRASG12C inhibitors, were compared between patients with LUADMuc and LUADnon-muc.
Methods
Study population
Adults with a histologically or cytologically confirmed diagnosis of LUAD seen at four academic institutions in the United States (Dana-Farber/Brigham and Women’s Cancer Center [DF/BWCC], MD Anderson Cancer Center [MDACC], Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center [MSKCC], and Massachusetts General Hospital [MGH]) and at one academic institution in Italy (University of Bologna, IRCCS Policlinico S.Orsola-Malpighi [Bologna]) between January 2001 and January 2024 were included in this study. All patients included had consented to Institutional Review Board-approved protocols.
Tumor histology was assessed by dedicated thoracic pathologists at each institution as part of standard clinical practice. IHC staining (e.g., TTF-1, p40, p63, napsin, cytokeratin 7) was carried out to confirm the epithelial lung origin of the tumor. Based on the pathology report, according to the WHO classification, LUAD cases were classified as LUADMuc or LUADnon-muc.4 LUADMuc cases were further classified into two categories: LUADMuc with mucinous features (LUADMuc-Features) if the pathologist reported mucinous features, signet ring cell features, or mixed mucinous and non-mucinous components; and pure LUADMuc (LUADMuc-Pure) if the pathologist reported “mucinous LUAD” or “invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma”.
Tumors with pleomorphic, sarcomatoid, epithelioid, spindle cell, giant cell, or neuroendocrine features were excluded. Tumors with multiple histologies, including adenosquamous carcinomas or combined adenocarcinoma and small cell lung carcinoma were also excluded.
Clinicopathologic, genomic, and immunophenotypic features were analyzed among patients in the DF/BWCC cohort. Transcriptomic features were analyzed through RNA sequencing data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) PanCancer Atlas cohort, available through cBioPortal (www.cbioportal.org).14–16 Treatment outcomes were obtained from five independent cohorts (DF/BWCC, MDACC, MSKCC, MGH, and Bologna).
All the clinical and pathological data analyzed were collected through manual chart review by medical oncologists or trained data abstractors.
For genomic analyses in patients with multiple tumor samples that underwent next-generation sequencing (NGS), duplicates were removed prioritizing samples analyzed with the most comprehensive NGS panel version and those that were collected closer to the initial cancer diagnosis.
For each analysis, cases missing data for the variable analyzed were excluded from the denominator. Additional methods related to PD-L1 expression scoring, tumor genomic profiling, multiplexed immunofluorescence, transcriptomic and statistical analyses are reported in the Supplementary Methods.
Results
Cohorts
Clinicopathologic, genomic, and immunophenotypic data analyzed in this study were obtained from the DF/BWCC cohort. Clinical outcomes of patients who received ICI alone and combined with chemotherapy were obtained from the DF/BWCC, MDACC, MSKCC, and Bologna cohorts. Clinical outcomes of patients who received KRASG12C inhibitors were available from the DF/BWCC, MSKCC, Bologna, and MGH cohorts. Transcriptional data were obtained from the publicly available The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) PanCancer Atlas LUAD dataset. Supplementary Figure S1 consists of the consort diagram outlining the various cohorts used in each part of this analysis.
Clinicopathologic characteristics of mucinous LUAD
Among 4,082 patients with LUAD in the DF/BWCC cohort, 90.1% (N=3,676) were classified as LUADnon-muc and 9.9% (N=406) as LUADMuc, of which 35.5% (N=144) were classified as LUADMuc-Pure and 64.5% (N=262) as LUADMuc-Features (Figure 1A). Compared to patients with LUADMuc, patients with LUADnon-muc, showed no differences in age at diagnosis, sex, self-reported race and ethnicity, and smoking status, but had a significantly lighter history of smoking (median pack-years: 15 vs 20, P=0.008), earlier stage of disease at diagnosis (stage I-III in 56.7% vs 43.8%, P<0.001) (Table 1), and lower PD-L1 TPS (median: 0% vs 5%, P<0.0001) (Figure 1B). Among patients diagnosed with stage I-III LUAD, patients with LUADMuc (N=230) had significantly shorter OS from diagnosis compared to patients with LUADnon-muc (N=1,325) (median: 80.2 vs 122.5 months; HR 1.43; 95% CI, 1.16–1.76; P=0.00095). Among patients diagnosed with stage IV LUAD, those with LUADMuc (N=176) exhibited significantly shorter OS from diagnosis than patients with LUADnon-muc (N=1,941) (median: 13.8 vs 26.4 months; HR 1.51; 95% CI, 1.27–1.78; P<0.0001) (Figure 1C). Among 1,193 patients evaluable for metastatic sites of disease at stage IV diagnosis, compared to LUADnon-muc (N=1,068), LUADMuc cases (N=125) had a lower frequency of brain metastasis (23.3% vs 41.9%, P<0.0001) and a higher frequency of intra-pulmonary metastasis (55.2% vs 36.9%, P<0.0001) (Figure 1D).

Molecular correlates of mucinous LUAD
Overall, 3,576 LUAD cases in the DF/BWCC cohort had successful DNA-based panel NGS data (OncoPanel, consisting of 447 cancer-associated genes); 89.6% (N=3,204) were LUADnon-muc and 10.4% (N=372) were LUADMuc. Tumor mutational burden (TMB) was lower in LUADMuc compared with LUADnon-muc (median: 6.8 vs 8.5 mut/Mb, P<0.0001) (Figure 1E). Qualitatively, LUADMuc, compared to LUADnon-muc, had a lower proportion of transversion (versus transition) mutations (median: 40% vs 50%, P<0.0001) (Supplementary Figure S2A–C), consistent with a lighter smoking history among patients with LUADMuc. Interestingly, the fraction of arm-level alterations (FAA), a measure of cancer aneuploidy whose high values have been correlated with worse outcomes to ICI in NSCLC, was significantly lower in LUADMuc compared to LUADnon-muc (median: 5.5% vs 8.7%, P<0.0001) (Supplementary Figure S3A).17 Additionally, LUADMuc cases were enriched in chromosome 15q amplifications (containing B2M, MAP2K1, IGF1R, RAD51, TP53BP1, and IDH2, among others) and 1p deletions (containing NOTCH1, NRAS, JAK1, CDKN2C, MTOR, MYCL, and ARID1A, among others) (Supplementary Figure S3B). Compared to LUADnon-muc, LUADMuc more commonly harbored KRAS driver mutations (57.5% vs 34.6%, P<0.0001) and ALK rearrangements (5.6% vs 2.6%, P=0.003), while less commonly carried EGFR (5.1% vs 24.3%, P<0.0001), BRAF (1.6% vs 4.8%, P=0.003), and MET (1.1% vs 3.1%, P=0.02) driver alterations (Figure 1F). When analyzing specific KRAS mutations, compared to LUADnon-muc, LUADMuc had a significantly higher prevalence of KRASG12D (16.4% vs 4.0%, P<0.0001), KRASG12V (13.7% vs 6.6%, P<0.0001), and KRASG12S (1.6% vs 0.5%, P=0.02) mutations (Supplementary Figure S4). Compared to LUADnon-muc, LUADMuc cases also had higher frequency of NKX2–1 (encoding TTF-1), STK11, SMARCA4, and GNAS mutations (q<0.05) and lower frequency of TP53, EGFR and BRAF mutations (q<0.05) (Figure 2A–B). In contrast to LUADnon-muc cases, KRAS mutations did not significantly co-occur with KEAP1 and SMARCA4 mutations in LUADMuc (Figure 2C). Mutations in NKX2–1 significantly co-occurred with KRAS and were mutually exclusive with STK11, KEAP1, and TP53 mutations only in LUADMuc cases (P<0.05). Conversely, NKX2–1 mutations significantly co-occurred with TP53 mutations in LUADnon-muc (P<0.05) (Figure 2C). These findings highlight that LUADMuc, compared to LUADnon-muc, has distinctive co-mutational patterns, such as a decreased association of KRAS/KEAP1, KRAS/SMARCA4, and potentially KRAS/STK11 mutations.
Immunophenotypic features of mucinous LUAD
Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) with the ImmunoProfile platform, measuring the density of intratumor CD8+, PD-1+, CD8+PD-1+, and FOXP3+ cells, was available in 502 unique LUAD cases, of which 10.2% (N=51) were LUADMuc and 89.8% (N=451) were LUADnon-muc (Supplementary Table S1). Compared to LUADnon-muc, LUADMuc had significantly lower intratumor CD8+ (median: 166.1 vs 194.3 cells/mm3, P=0.02) and FOXP3+ cells (median: 44.0 vs 68.0 cells/mm3, P=0.007) (Figure 3A). Since most of LUADMuc cases profiled had stage I-III disease (86.3% vs 64.1% in LUADnon-muc, P=0.003), we then restricted the analyses to stage I-III LUAD and observed consistent findings: LUADMuc cases (N=44), compared to LUADnon-muc (N=289), had significantly lower intratumor CD8+ (median: 167.0 vs 250.0 cells/mm3, P<0.0001), PD-1+ (median: 80.0 vs 112.4 cells/mm3, P=0.03), CD8+PD-1+ (median: 13.3 vs 21.0 cells/mm3, P=0.03), and FOXP3+ cells (median: 41.5 vs 70.8 cells/mm3, P=0.001) (Figure 3B). Representative images of KRASG12D-mutated LUADMuc and LUADnon-muc cases are shown in Figure 3C, highlighting a more pronounced immune cell infiltration in the LUADnon-muc case.
Outcomes to immunotherapy in patients with mucinous LUAD
Among a total of 1,623 patients with metastatic LUAD who received ICIs, 112 were classified as LUADMuc and 1,511 as LUADnon-muc. A total of 1,551 (95.6%) patients received PD-(L)1 blockade monotherapy, and 72 (4.4%) patients received combined CTLA4/PD-(L)1 blockade therapy. The median follow-up time was similar between LUADMuc and LUADnon-muc cases (44.6 vs 46.0 months, P=0.30). As expected, compared to patients with LUADnon-muc, patients with LUADMuc were more likely to have no smoking history (24.8% vs 16.4%, P=0.03), had lower PD-L1 TPS (median: 1% vs 50%, P<0.001), and a different distribution of driver genomic alterations (P<0.001), mainly due to a higher prevalence of KRAS mutations (58.2% vs 38.4%) and lower frequency of EGFR mutations (0.9% vs 8.9%) (Supplementary Table S2). No significant imbalances in age, sex, line of treatment, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS), and type of treatment were observed. An overview of baseline patient characteristics in each cohort is reported in Supplementary Table S3, while treatment outcomes by cohort are shown in Supplementary Figure S5. Compared to patients with LUADnon-muc, patients with LUADMuc had significantly lower objective response rate (ORR) (8.4% vs 25.9%, P<0.0001), and shorter median progression-free survival (mPFS: 2.6 vs 3.9 months; HR: 1.52, P<0.0001) and median overall survival (mOS: 9.9 vs 17.2 months; HR: 1.57, P<0.0001) (Figure 4A–C). After adjusting for potential confounders in a multivariable Cox-regression model including age, sex, smoking status, PD-L1 TPS, genomic driver alteration, line of treatment, and baseline ECOG PS, LUADMuc retained a significant association with worse PFS (HR: 1.28; 95% CI, 1.02–1.61; P=0.03) and OS (HR: 1.47; 95% CI, 1.15–1.85; P=0.002) (Supplementary Figure S6).
Outcomes to chemoimmunotherapy in patients with mucinous LUAD
A total of 1,307 patients with metastatic LUAD received ICI plus chemotherapy, 140 of which were classified as LUADMuc and 1,167 as LUADnon-muc. A total of 1,286 (98.4%) patients received PD-(L)1 blockade and platinum-based chemotherapy, and 21 (1.6%) patients also received bevacizumab. The median follow-up time was similar between LUADMuc and LUADnon-muc cases (28.3 vs 24.2 months, P=0.84). Again, compared to patients with LUADnon-muc, patients with LUADMuc had lower PD-L1 TPS (median: 0% vs 1%, P<0.001) and a different distribution of driver genomic alterations (P<0.001), mainly due to a higher prevalence of KRAS mutations (62.4% vs 38.5%) and lower prevalence of EGFR mutations (1.5% vs 6.2%). No significant imbalances in age, sex, smoking status, line of treatment, ECOG PS, and type of treatment were observed (Supplementary Table S4). An overview of baseline patient characteristics in each cohort is reported in Supplementary Table S5, while treatment outcomes by cohort are shown in Supplementary Figure S7. Compared to patients with LUADnon-muc, patients with LUADMuc had significantly lower ORR (21.3% vs 38.5%, P<0.0001), and shorter PFS (median: 5.0 vs 7.0 months; HR: 1.52, P<0.0001) and OS (median: 11.4 vs 19.6 months; HR: 1.54, P<0.0001) (Figure 4D–F). After adjusting for potential confounders in a multivariable Cox-regression model including age, sex, smoking status, PD-L1 TPS, genomic driver alteration, line of treatment, and baseline ECOG PS, LUADMuc retained a significant association with worse PFS (HR: 1.35; 95% CI, 1.06–1.69; P=0.01) and OS (HR: 1.37; 95% CI, 1.06–1.79; P=0.01) (Supplementary Figure S8).
Outcomes to KRASG12C inhibitors in patients with mucinous LUAD
Among 168 patients with metastatic LUAD who received KRASG12C inhibitors (adagrasib or sotorasib), 18 were classified as LUADMuc and 150 as LUADnon-muc. No significant imbalances in baseline characteristics were observed, including age, sex, smoking status, line of treatment, ECOG PS, and type of treatment (Supplementary Table S6). An overview of baseline patient characteristics in each cohort is reported in Supplementary Table S7. Compared to patients with LUADnon-muc, patients with LUADMuc had numerically lower ORR (16.7% vs 34.9%, P=0.12), numerically shorter PFS (median: 4.6 vs 5.6 months; HR: 1.47, P=0.16) and significantly shorter OS (median: 6.8 vs 10.8 months; HR: 2.00, P=0.018) (Figure 4G–I).
Correlates of KRAS mutations and impact on ICI outcomes in patients with mucinous LUAD
Given that KRAS is the most common driver in LUADMuc cases, accounting for 57.5% of cases (Figure 1F), we next explored the impact of these mutations to a deeper extent. Patients with KRAS-mutated LUADMuc (KRASMUT-LUADMuc), compared to patients with KRAS wild-type LUADMuc (KRASWT-LUADMuc), were older (median: 68 vs 66 years, P=0.04), had a higher pack-year smoking history (median pack-years: 15 vs 10, P=0.04), and were more likely diagnosed with stage I-III disease than stage IV (64.3% vs 50.3%, P=0.01) (Supplementary Table S8). PD-L1 TPS was similar between KRASMUT-LUADMuc and KRASWT-LUADMuc (median: 0.0% vs 0.0%, P=0.73); however, KRASMUT-LUADMuc showed higher TMB (median: 7.6 vs 6.1 mut/Mb, P=0.004), lower FAA (median: 4.3% vs 7.4%, P=0.004), higher frequency of STK11, NKX2–1, MGA, and GNAS mutations, and lower frequency of TP53, EGFR, and ERBB2 mutations (q<0.15) (Supplementary Figure S9A–D). Among KRAS mutations, KRASG12D was found highly enriched in LUADMuc, questioning whether its presence could further differentiate KRASMUT-LUADMuc cases. Patients with KRASG12D-LUADMuc, compared to patients with KRASnon-G12D-LUADMuc, more frequently had no smoking history (40.0% vs 16.3%, P<0.001), had lower pack-years (median: 7.5 vs 22.0, P=0.008), and more commonly presented with stage I-III at diagnosis (76.7% vs 59.5%, P=0.03) (Supplementary Table S9). In addition, KRASG12D-LUADMuc, compared with KRASnon-G12D-LUADMuc, had lower PD-L1 TPS (median: 0.0% vs 2.0%, P=0.002), lower TMB (median: 6.1 vs 7.6 mut/Mb, P=0.009), lower FAA (median: 1.4% vs 5.3%, P=0.02), higher frequency of GNAS mutations and lower frequency of STK11 mutations (q<0.15) (Supplementary Figure S9E–H). Lastly, we explored ICI outcomes among patients with LUADMuc evaluable for KRAS mutational status. No unexpected imbalances in baseline characteristics were observed between groups (Supplementary Table S10). Compared to KRASWT-LUADMuc (N=47), KRASMUT-LUADMuc (N=64) achieved similar ORR (11.7% vs 4.4%, P=0.18), but significantly longer PFS (median: 3.8 vs 1.9 months, HR 0.46, P=0.0002) and OS (median: 14.0 vs 6.0 months, HR 0.57, P=0.008) (Supplementary Figure S10A–C). By contrast, comparing KRASWT-LUADMuc (N=50) and KRASMUT-LUADMuc (N=81), those who received combination ICI and chemotherapy (Supplementary Table S11) showed similar outcomes (Supplementary Figure S10D–F).
Impact of STK11, KEAP1, and SMARCA4 mutations on ICI outcomes in patients with mucinous LUAD
Mutations in STK11, KEAP1, and SMARCA4, which have been associated with poor ICI efficacy in patients with NSCLC, were found enriched in LUADMuc (Figure 2A–B).18–22 To understand the impact these mutations had on the worse outcomes observed in LUADMuc cases, we investigated whether LUADMuc was still associated with worse outcomes to ICI only compared to LUADnon-muc among cases harboring mutations in at least one gene among STK11, KEAP1, or SMARCA4 (STK11MUT and/or KEAP1MUT and/or SMARCA4MUT). No unexpected imbalances in baseline characteristics between the two groups were observed (Supplementary Table S12). Even in the population of patients with LUAD and a mutation in at least one gene among STK11, KEAP1, and SMARCA4, patients with LUADMuc achieved significantly worse ORR, PFS, and OS compared to patients with LUADnon-muc (Supplementary Figure S11). In addition, even among LUADMuc cases, the presence of a mutation in STK11, KEAP1 or SMARCA4 was associated with shorter survival outcomes in patients who received ICI (Supplementary Figure S12). This suggests that the enrichment of these mutations is associated with a worse response to ICI in LUADMuc. However, they only partially account for the worse outcomes to ICI in these patients.
Characteristics of LUADMuc-Pure and LUADMuc-Features
Among LUADMuc cases, we investigated whether patients with LUADMuc-Pure and LUADMuc-Features had distinctive clinicopathologic and genomic features and showed different response to treatments. Compared to patients with LUADMuc-Features, patients with LUADMuc-Pure had similar age at diagnosis and sex, a higher proportion of patients with no smoking history (37.5% vs 21.1%, P<0.001; median: 7 vs 20 pack-years, P=0.002), and more frequently presented with stage I-III disease at diagnosis (66.7% vs 51.1%, P=0.004) (Supplementary Table S13). In addition, compared to patients with LUADMuc-Features, LUADMuc-Pure cases had lower PD-L1 TPS (median: 0% vs 1%, P=0.008), TMB (median: 6.1 vs 7.6 mut/Mb, P<0.0001), FAA (median: 2% vs 8%, P<0.0001), and were enriched in NKX2–1, KRAS (especially KRASG12D), and GNAS mutations, but depleted in TP53, KEAP1, and STK11 mutations (q<0.15) (Figure 5A–E). Among 125 patients with LUADMuc evaluable for metastatic sites of disease at stage IV diagnosis, compared to LUADMuc-Features (N=92), LUADMuc-Pure cases (N=33) had a lower frequency of brain metastasis (6.3% vs 29.5%, P=0.015) and bone metastasis (33.3% vs 55.4%, P=0.048), and a higher frequency of intra-pulmonary metastasis (78.8% vs 46.7%, P=0.003) (Figure 5F). When evaluating the OS from diagnosis in patients with stage I-III LUADMuc, compared to patients with LUADMuc-Features (N=134), patients with LUADMuc-Pure (N=96) had significantly longer OS (median: 157.3 vs 63.8 months; HR 0.44; 95% CI, 0.28–0.68; P=0.0003); similarly, among patients diagnosed with stage IV LUADMuc, those with LUADMuc-Pure (N=48) exhibited significantly longer OS from diagnosis than patients with LUADMuc-Features (N=128) (median: 22.0 vs 12.1 months; HR 0.69; 95% CI, 0.48–1.00; P=0.0497) (Figure 5G). Among patients with LUADMuc who received ICI only, compared to patients with LUADMuc-Features (N=72), patients with LUADMuc-Pure (N=40) (Supplementary Table S14) had lower ORR (0% vs 13%, P=0.02), similar PFS (median: 3.3 vs 2.1 months, HR 0.86, P=0.46), and longer OS (median: 20.9 vs 6.9 months, HR 0.56, P=0.01) (Supplementary Figure S13A–C). When evaluating the outcomes to ICI plus chemotherapy, compared to patients with LUADMuc-Features (N=94), patients with LUADMuc-Pure (N=46) (Supplementary Table S15) had similar ORR (23.3% vs 20.4%, P=0.71) and PFS (median: 7.8 vs 4.8 months, HR 0.89, P=0.54), and again showed longer OS (median: 19.0 vs 9.0 months, HR 0.39, P=0.03) (Supplementary Figure S13D–F). This suggests that while LUADMuc-Pure has a more indolent nature it may not be responsive to ICI.
Transcriptional subtypes of mucinous LUAD in the TCGA LUAD cohort
Publicly available pathology reports from TCGA PanCancer Atlas were used to manually annotate LUADMuc and LUADnon-muc cases.14–16 Among 476 unique LUAD cases with RNA sequencing data, 7.1% (N=34) were LUADMuc and 92.9% (N=442) were LUADnon-muc. To assess whether LUADMuc could be further classified with a different gene expression repertoire, we first carried out differential gene expression analysis comparing LUADMuc versus LUADnon-muc to retrieve the top upregulated genes in LUADMuc. Given the different size of the compared groups, a resampling procedure was applied by randomly splitting the LUADnon-muc population into five subgroups. Only genes differentially expressed in all the differential gene expression analyses were considered. Once the transcriptional hallmark of LUADMuc was identified, unsupervised hierarchical clustering was carried out. In this way, we identified two different clusters of LUADMuc: LUADMuc-High (N=11), with relatively higher expression of LUADMuc-related genes, and LUADMuc-Low (N=23), with relatively lower expression of LUADMuc-related genes (Supplementary Figure S14). Compared to patients with LUADMuc-Low, patients with LUADMuc-High showed no differences in age at diagnosis and sex, but had lower TMB (median: 2.5 vs 3.8 mut/Mb, P=0.03), lower aneuploidy as measured by fraction of genome altered (median: 0.2% vs 1.8%, P=0.001), numerically different frequencies of mutations in the top 10 mutated genes in LUADMuc, a different distribution of immune subtypes mainly characterized by a lower proportion of the desert subtype (P<0.0001), and longer OS from diagnosis (median: 39.4 vs 32.1 months, P=0.04) (Supplementary Figure S15). Collectively, these observations suggest a certain degree of heterogeneity in the context of LUADMuc cases.
Discussion
We found that mucinous histology is seen in 10% of lung adenocarcinomas and exhibits distinctive clinical, molecular, and pathological features. LUADMuc cases had a lower cigarette smoking history, PD-L1 expression, and TMB, all of which are features associated with decreased ICI efficacy. We also observed a shorter OS from diagnosis among patients with LUADMuc, regardless of the stage of disease, highlighting the limited prognosis of this histologic subtype. A “spread through air spaces” (STAS) invasion pattern on histology is thought to be associated with worse prognosis in early-stage LUAD. STAS was observed in 70% of resected invasive mucinous adenocarcinomas in previous studies, compared to 15–48% of LUADnon-muc cases.23,24 Although we did not assess the prevalence of STAS in our cohort, we observed that patients with early stage of disease (I-III) diagnosed with LUADMuc have a worse prognosis than those with LUADnon-muc.
Additionally, we observed a significant enrichment of KRAS, NKX2–1, GNAS, STK11, and SMARCA4 mutations among LUADMuc cases.13 STK11 and SMARCA4 mutations, which have been associated with worse outcomes to treatment, can contribute in explaining the unfavorable prognosis observed in patients with LUADMuc.18–22 A combined analysis of both mutations (e.g. STK11, SMARCA4 mutation status) and histologic features may better predict treatment response in LUAD.
Notably, our study is the first to report worse outcomes with ICI-based therapies in patients with LUADMuc compared to those with LUADnon-muc. Previous studies had suggested reduced ICI efficacy in LUADMuc due to low PD-L1 TPS values. 25–27 In a study of four patients with invasive mucinous LUAD, PD-L1 was <1% in all cases, while two other studies including 33 and 31 invasive mucinous LUAD cases showed a PD-L1 ≥1% in only 6.1% and 9.7%, respectively.25–27 Our significantly larger cohort also found that LUADMuc is associated with lower PD-L1 TPS; in addition, we observed a significantly lower TMB and intratumoral immune cell density, factors that are all associated with diminished response to ICI therapies, in LUADMuc compared to LUADnon-muc.28–30 These features are likely all interconnected with each other, as lighter history of tobacco use, lower TMB values, and mutations in genes such as STK11 and KEAP1, which characterize LUADMuc cases, have been consistently associated with lower tumor immunogenicity in previous studies.19,28,31,32 This observation further suggests that in addition to LUADMuc carrying a worse overall prognosis, it is also less responsive to current ICI-based treatments. In our cohort, outcomes to KRASG12C inhibitors were similarly worse in patients LUADMuc, who achieved a statistically significant shorter OS. Although a larger cohort is needed to confirm this observation, it reinforces the notion that LUADMuc is a hard-to-treat LUAD subtype.
Among LUADMuc, patients with LUADMuc-Pure also had distinct clinicopathologic (lower association with cigarette smoking history, different distribution of sites of metastasis, lower PD-L1 TPS) and genomic features (lower TMB; depleted in TP53, KEAP1, and STK11 mutations), and had a better natural history compared to patients with LUADMuc-Features.
While a minority of patients with advanced LUADMuc-Features responded to ICI, patients with advanced LUADMuc-Pure showed no response to ICI but had longer OS to both ICIs only and combined with chemotherapy. This suggests that despite ICI-insensitivity, LUADMuc-Pure might be a slower-growing subtype of LUAD. Biologically, an almost complete lack of PD-L1 expression, lower TMB, and enrichment for an ICI-unresponsive KRAS mutation (KRASG12D) may explain the lack of activity of ICI only in this subgroup.33 A lower frequency of bad prognostic features such as brain metastasis and mutations in STK11 and KEAP1 may partially explain the longer OS in LUADMuc-Pure cases compared to LUADMuc-Features ones. These hypotheses will need to be tested in larger cohorts of LUADMuc-Pure vs LUADMuc-Features. Nonetheless, this suggests that the presence and extent of mucinous histology should be considered in prognostication and prediction.
Our unbiased transcriptional analysis of LUADMuc using TCGA data found an association between transcriptional features, genotype, and prognosis consistent with our histology-based analysis. Cases with relatively high expression of LUADMuc-related genes, namely LUADMuc-High, had characteristics and outcomes similar to LUADMuc-Pure, including lower TMB and aneuploidy levels, higher frequency of KRAS, NKX2–1, and GNAS mutations and lower frequency of STK11, KEAP1, and SMARCA4 mutations, and longer OS from diagnosis. Conversely, LUADMuc cases with relatively low expression of LUADMuc-related genes, namely LUADMuc-Low, demonstrated characteristics more similar to those of LUADMuc-Features.
These findings have immediate implications in clinical practice. LUADMuc histology should be considered when stratifying whether patients should receive ICI therapy, especially when developing clinical trials for LUAD. We found that KRAS driver mutations identified a population of patients with LUADMuc with distinctive clinicopathologic and genomic features and greater benefit from ICI. Furthermore, our data suggest the presence of significant clinicopathologic, genomic, and outcomes differences between LUADMuc-Pure and LUADMuc-Features, suggesting that mixed mucinous histology is a distinct entity compared to pure mucinous histology.
The main limitation of this study is the lack of complete data for all patients included. In addition, a centralized pathology review was not practical given the retrospective design of the study and the involvement of five institution across Europe and the United States. Variations in classifying LUAD cases across different institutions may be a limitation in comparing cohorts. However, we consistently found worse outcomes among LUADMuc cases even when we analyzed cohorts separately. Moreover, as this study aims to provide guidance in real-world clinical practice scenarios, cases with any mucinous component were included in the LUADMuc category, while the distinction between LUADMuc-Pure and LUADMuc-Features was a secondary analysis. Additionally, the unavailability of targeted RNA fusion testing precluded our ability to assess the role of NRG1 fusions, which have previously been reported to be enriched in LUADMuc.7,12 Nevertheless, the strengths of this study include the large sample size, the comprehensive characterization of LUAD cases using a large genomic panel and a multiplexed immunofluorescence platform, and the consistent results observed among several independent cohorts from academic centers.
The current study identifies LUADMuc as a harder-to-treat subtype of LUAD with distinctive clinicopathologic, genomic, immunophenotypic, and transcriptional characteristics that contribute to its worse response to existing treatments. Within LUADMuc, histologic subtypes (LUADMuc-Pure vs LUADMuc-Features) and the presence of specific mutations (e.g., KRAS, STK11, KEAP1, or SMARCA4 mutations) influences treatment outcomes. Physicians and investigators should consider the presence and extent of mucinous histology in lung adenocarcinomas to prognosticate and predict the relative clinical benefit of ICI-based and KRASG12C inhibitor therapies.

Highlights.
Approximately 10% of lung adenocarcinomas (LUAD) have a mucinous component (LUADMuc).
Compared to non-mucinous LUAD (LUADnon-muc), LUADMuc was associated to lighter smoking history and lower PD-L1 expression.
LUADMuc had lower tumor mutation burden and more KRAS, STK11, SMARCA4, NKX2–1, and GNAS mutations than LUADnon-muc.
Intratumor CD8+, PD-1+, CD8+PD-1+, and FOXP3+ cell density was lower in LUADMuc compared to LUADnon-muc.
Patients with LUADMuc had poorer outcomes to immunotherapy +/− chemotherapy and KRASG12C inhibitors than LUADnon-muc.
